doc.title: Phil Flanigan interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 15, 1998

title: Acoustic bass versus pickups and the stick bass
summary: He argues an acoustic bass should sound acoustic, and discusses the stick bass and Bob Cranshaw's travel bass.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: You can be a musician and not have any technical knowledge and know the serial numbers and model numbers of all the various different equipment, like an AV 20 and blah, blah, blah — an AKG, a 4756, and on from there — but the engineers may know all that and it’s pretty useless data really when you get right down to it if you don’t know what you’re listening to, if you can’t recognize a sound. It sounds simple, doesn’t it?
And what’s appropriate for different musical situations‚ that a bass sound should be more authentic for this particular situation you were in than processed.
Right. Well I’m not sure I understand the question.
I don’t think there was a question there.

Yeah, okay. Well I can go off from there, because if it’s an acoustic bass, it should be acoustic. Bing. The thing was made with this big piece of wood for a reason. That’s so the wood moves the air, not so that it moves some little Piezo electric invaders that were stuck into the bridge to induce small currents to be amplified later, and then have a conical paper cone pushing air at an unwilling audience — unwitting and often unwilling audience. I don’t see why you have to carry around all that wood if you’re just going to pretend it’s not there. If you want to heavily amplify your upright bass, get one of those stick things that has no body, that has no wood plates if you will, like the top of the bass, the part that moves and creates the sound, moves the air. If you don’t have that and you’re not using it, why not just admit defeat and play a stick.
Play a stick. Did you ever play a stick?
Yeah I have on a number of occasions. It’s very, it’s sort of like kissing through a screen door or something like that.

It’s a little alien for me. It’s different — I really don’t like it because there’s no shoulder here, so you never have to really go into thumb position. Thumb position is this thing, where you’re putting the thumb on a string and fingering up above it. You don’t have to © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -10-
do that because there’s no — you can just go up like this and it’s different, a really a very different instrument.
Isn’t it hard — can you lean your body against it somehow?

They have little struts and things that you can collapse for easy storage. It reminds me of an exercise machine you throw under your bed, this kind of thing. Bob Cranshaw has a good one though, that he had custom made for him, which is a bass — well it’s a stick but it’s got more of a cavity, like maybe a shoe box or slightly larger size piece of wood that’s hollow. It has some resonance factor to it, so the bridge is not just sitting on a block of wood, it’s something solid. So it moves a little bit. So it probably sounds better. But he’s got it hinged — the neck — he’s got it hinged so he can collapse the neck down, loosen the strings, loosen the thing on the neck, collapse it down and it all fits in a little duffel bag sized case that you can bring on an airplane or throw it in the overhead, or I guess probably just check it. It’s the only one - he’s got the only one.
I don’t know. You’d have to ask him.
